title: How Nscale’s Unbuilt Data Centers Undercut Its $35 Billion IPO Pitch
summary: AI chip rental business Nscale, which has filed paperwork indicating its plan to go public, is a puny, relatively new entrant in the neocloud race. At first blush, it looks to hold a lot of promise, posting rapid growth in the past year and boasting a backlog of contracted revenue on par with that of older rival CoreWeave. But nearly all of Nscale’s $103 billion in contract commitments rely on data centers it hasn’t yet built—or even raised all the money needed to build. That makes Nscale a symbol of the risks inherent in the AI boom. It also suggests the $35 billion valuation for which it is reportedly aiming in its initial public offering looks far too rich. The right valuation is probably less than half that.

title: How Investors Are Financing On-Site Power to Break AI Bottlenecks
summary: Companies building and operating data centers are hungry for ways to secure the power needed to move ahead with massive AI build-outs. That’s prompted big financing pledges and creative dealmaking for on-site power that can cut data centers’ reliance on electric grids. Investors are getting in on the crunch through several angles, including large investments in specific projects, such as new on-site power plants. Some investors are also taking equity stakes in companies that provide on-site power, or providing outside capital to finance equipment like fuel cells for end customers such as AI cloud providers. A Blackstone-led group, including KKR and Apollo, this summer agreed to invest $5.3 billion for a 49% stake in five gas-fired power projects pipeline giant Williams is developing to supply on-site power for data centers. Of the $5.3 billion, $4.4 billion will cover the investors’ share of expected project costs, Williams said. Though on-site power can be pricier than connecting to the grid, availability and speed is an obvious advantage. Williams, which recently expanded into developing and running on-site generation for data centers, said last month it brought its first 200 megawatts online less than 18 months after commercialization. By comparison, Fitch Ratings estimates that building new infrastructure such as grid-connected power plants and high-voltage transmission lines can take five to 10 years. Many power-generation deals have been financed primarily on a project-by-project basis. But some investors have also started buying stakes in companies that provide on-site power generation, whether that be gas plants, fuel cells or solar projects, giving investors exposure to broader growth rather than a specific project. For instance, Blackstone and Halliburton in May announced a $1 billion equity investment in VoltaGrid, which builds and operates on-site gas-powered systems for data centers. “With all the private equity and other money that has come into the market, there’s different structures. And when there’s private equity, they want to have an ownership interest in the developer entity,” said Carl Bivens, a real estate partner at Troutman Pepper Locke. Meanwhile, the up-front costs of bringing power on-site to data centers quickly has created a need for outside capital to provide financing for customers such as smaller AI cloud providers. That’s similar to other areas in AI infrastructure, where some cloud providers have been relying on special purpose vehicles that use outside capital to finance expensive assets like graphics processing units. On the power side, Bloom Energy announced last fall that Brookfield Asset Management had agreed to provide up to $5 billion to finance future power projects for AI data centers, with Bloom providing the fuel cells. In June, Bloom announced that Brookfield had expanded the amount of potential financing to $25 billion. Bloom has relied for more than a decade on infrastructure funds and investment firms to form SPVs that finance deployments of its products, but investor interest accelerated more recently, a person familiar with the financings said. Investors are also financing on-site power projects for Bloom customers, separately from the broader Brookfield framework. In July, project developer Industrial Development Funding and investment firm Oaktree Capital Management announced a $1.7 billion project investment to install Bloom fuel cells at Nebius data centers. Oaktree is contributing minority equity financing, with MUFG leading senior debt financing, while Nebius will pay Bloom for power. But the rush of financing for on-site power creates a potential timing mismatch across different parts of what’s needed to get an AI data center up and running. Some power assets can operate for decades, while big AI compute contracts are often much shorter and the GPUs inside data centers can become outdated in just a few years. For developers and the investors financing power infrastructure, longer contracts that lock in predictable cash flow are preferable. Investors are pushing for longer customer commitments to underpin these deals, increasingly favoring 10- to 15-year commitments from large cloud providers with five-year renewal options, Bivens said. “It provides a longer runway of guaranteed rent for the investors. It allows [institutional investors] to amortize their costs of the behind-the-meter solution or the data center build,” he said. Customers of the on-site power may want more flexibility, particularly if they’re awaiting grid power. That points to the bigger question of how much data centers will need to rely on on-site power in the long term. For example, more grid power could become available or GPUs could become more energy efficient, and data centers’ on-site power needs might evolve by the time big contracts expire. Industrial Development Funding, an infrastructure investment firm and the developer behind the Bloom-Nebius project, says on-site power projects can still be valuable even if the data centers’ power needs themselves change. The owners of the project could sell power into broader markets down the line, said IDF CEO Nik Nunes. For instance, if a data center tenant moves on when its initial contract term ends, the power asset could be mostly paid off but could still generate revenue. "If I have a power block that is significantly amortized in six to eight years, I have a lot of optionality to sell that power into the grid or into other markets,” Nunes said. Converting to Convertibles Convertible bonds have been one particularly popular way for tech companies to raise cash in a banner year for financing across the sector, fueled by the AI build-out. Technology companies have accounted for about 60% of overall U.S. convertible bond issuance so far in 2026, raising roughly $78 billion through Sept. 11, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. That’s up from around 44% of that market last year. By comparison, tech companies accounted for 50% of equity follow-on offerings, 27% of investment-grade debt and 20% of high-yield issuance so far this year. The convertible surge comes as financing costs for AI-specific debt have been rising . Investors are swamped with new supply and grappling with uncertainties about how AI investments will pay off. Convertible debt often carries lower coupons than straight corporate bonds since investors get an upside if the stock rises. That can eventually dilute the holdings of existing shareholders, but potentially less so than equity offerings. “Obviously, there’s the benefits of being not as dilutive as a follow-on. So it has been one of the places of priority,” Chris Fenske, head of capital markets research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said on a webinar last week. And S&P Global’s total doesn’t count recent convertible issuance like CoreWeave’s $4.2 billion sale last week. But as more companies tap convertibles, that form of financing too could get more expensive—we’ll see whether those firms shift to equity raises next. Proximal raised its seed round at the end of last year, when it was generating a negligible amount of revenue, co-founder and CEO Calvin Chen said. Chen had cofounded the 40-person startup last fall with his roommate Justus Mattern , who previously worked at compute startup Prime Intellect , which itself is only two years old. title: Use Google Gemini to Research Vendor Products, Services, and Features
summary: Making a vendor recommendation for a major IT initiative can be paralyzing. Every company promises a “seamless” user experience and “robust” APIs, but buyers typically lack visibility into real-world implementation and operations until after they’ve already made a decision. As a result, many tech leaders default to recommendations from people in their networks, or even avoid making a change at all, preferring to stick with the “devil they know” over risking the unknown. Google Gemini can help you quickly research vendor products, services, and features, going beyond the marketing materials to surface real-world insights about implementation, integration, and total cost of ownership. Step 1: Vent Your Frustrations Open up a new chat in Gemini and list off everything that is driving you mad about your current product or platform so Gemini has comprehensive context about the problem you are looking to solve. If you’re looking for a new cloud vendor, the problem might be unpredictable costs, or it might be unacceptable levels of latency. Those are two very different problems, and each might be best solved by two different vendors. Don’t sugar-coat here. Mention user adoption issues, unhelpful account managers, broken integrations, and anything else that has you considering a change. If Gemini knows what’s currently going wrong, it will be better equipped to make best-fit recommendations. Step 2: Generate Recommendations Give Gemini some basic background information about your company and what technology you’re looking to replace. Include your frustrations from Step 1. Here’s a sample prompt: I am the CIO at [company]. We are currently evaluating vendor options to [replatform our intranet]. Right now, we use [vendor], but we are looking to switch because [we are unhappy with limited functionality and account support]. Suggest additional vendor options to consider and include descriptions of their product and services and key features. Gemini will evaluate the scope of the change you are looking to make, consider your specific context, and offer several options. If you explain that you lead the IT department at a global supply chain company with 14,000 employees, for example, Gemini will account for organization-specific considerations like mobile access and integration with shift-scheduling systems. Review Gemini’s initial shortlist to identify top contenders, eliminate any obvious mismatches, and move forward with your finalists. Step 3: Dig Deeper Gemini’s initial responses will focus on the hero features and selling points of several options, drawing from various sources, including vendors’ own marketing materials. This means you may need to continue the conversation to fully address potential friction points like integration, pricing issues, and scalability challenges. Follow up with Gemini, this time asking it to take a more skeptical look at your top choices. Here, you can ask pointed questions about specific details and more fully explore likely total costs. You can even prompt Gemini to scour the web for user reviews, helping you to discover stories from previous customers who had subpar experiences. Try prompts like these: What are some of the known integration challenges when connecting [Vendor] to [System A] and [System B]? Summarize the three most common complaints that enterprise IT teams express about [Vendor’s] technical performance or customer service. What is the realistic enterprise deployment timeline for [Vendor], as opposed to their estimated sales timeline? Are there any configuration issues I should watch out for? By asking these types of questions, you can push Gemini to go beyond generic feature lists and give you more granular information that gets you closer to a decision. Step 4: Compare and Contrast Chat with Gemini for a bit. Go back-and-forth until you feel like you have a comprehensive understanding of the benefits and potential tradeoffs for each vendor, including how each will fit with your existing environment. Then, ask Gemini to summarize its findings in a structured table. Try this prompt: Create a matrix comparing [Vendor A] and [Vendor B] across deployment timeline, integration complexity, and potential friction points. Gemini will generate a clean table that helps you cut through the weeds of your sprawling research session, take a big-picture view of your options, and more clearly how vendors compare with one another on your most important criteria. You and your team will still need to make the final recommendation to your leadership team. But now, you will have the real-world information you need to help you make (and defend) your choice.

title: Microsoft Tears Down Its AI Data Wall
summary: Microsoft’s biggest products have generally thrived by letting other companies build on top of them. So Microsoft’s decision to join Apache Ossie, a 1-year-old software industry group aiming to make it easier for AI tools to access data from applications and databases, might not seem like a big deal. But actually it is. Just four months ago, Microsoft moved to block partners from connecting their data management tools to Microsoft’s Power BI, which companies use to analyze data in charts and graphs. In doing so, Microsoft appeared to be protecting its own data management product, Fabric, at the expense of rival firms such as Databricks and Snowflake. In other words, Microsoft was opening a new front in the AI data wars, part of traditional enterprise app firms’ efforts to stop customers from using AI from other companies to access data they store in traditional apps. After our report in May, Microsoft took heat for its decision. We don’t know what’s happened behind the scenes since then, but the company must have had a change of heart. And its decision to join Ossie is in line with CEO Satya Nadella’s strategy of building products that worked those of rivals, such as developing a mobile version of Office for Apple iOS and Google’s Android operating systems over a decade ago. Salesforce made a similar transition in the past couple of years and now is making it easy for customers to use AI tools such as Claude to access their Salesforce data—for a price.
